blogs.title: The Subjective Observer Standard: Reinterpreting 'Transformative Use' Post-*Warhol*
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Second Circuit's critical application of the "purpose and character" factor in *Santos v. Kimmel*, specifically focusing on the court's rejection of George Santos's argument regarding his own subjective intent versus the "reasonable observer's" perspective on Kimmel's parody. It examines how the decision reinforces the *Goldsmith* precedent by distinguishing the original artistic purpose of a Cameo video from a secondary, mocking use, and discusses the implications for attorneys defending satire against claims of non-transformative appropriation.

blogs.title: Market Harm in Parody: Applying the *Hachette* Test to Late-Night Commentary
blogs.description: Focusing on the 4th fair use factor, this blog post breaks down the Second Circuit's reasoning on market harm or devaluation. It explains why the court accepted the District Court's position that a critical mockery of a video does not "usurp" the market for a potential licensee to cause a "competing substitute," drawing links between this ruling and broader trends in defining the licensing market for creative versus communicative works.

blogs.title: Who Owns the Cameo Platform? Third-Party Liability and Contractual Preemption
blogs.description: This piece isolates the contract claims, analyzing the Second Circuit's dismissal of George Santos's breach and fraudulent inducement claims. It details the court's application of Illinois and New York law regarding "third-party beneficiaries" in Terms of Service and why the lack of "express declaration" barred the plaintiff from claiming a contractual duty to comply with platform rules, a significant development for user-content platform liability.
